transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ben (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Zoe (Redwood SE), Carlos (Atlas ML), Priya (Atlas Infra), Tom (Atlas CTO), Aisha (Atlas Security)

Summary (auto-ish):
Ben: quick recap, this is to validate that JSON mode and tool-calling won't blow our latency SLOs. we want deterministic json outputs that we can parse, and also to measure the extra overhead when we force constrained decoding.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ben: alright good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick intros, then maya will walk through our runtime behavior with JSON mode and function calling.
[00:18] Carlos: hey, Carlos here. main goal: we have a payment-fraud assistant that needs structured JSON outputs for decisioning pipelines, latency < 250ms p50 and < 600ms p95, from ingestion to structured result. also need to run in our VPC or on-prem eventually.
[00:34] Maya: thanks Carlos. just to set expectations: constrained decoding (aka JSON mode) requires the model to only emit tokens that lead to syntactically valid JSON. we implement that at the token level during decoding which means additional CPU/GPU logic per step.
[00:50] Tom: is that like beam search with grammar? what's the perf hit?
[00:56] Maya: good q. we don't use heavy beam search; typically we run greedy or top-k with constraints. the overhead comes from lookups to the constraint automaton (we compile grammar / JSON schemas into a token-valid set or prefix tree). that check is O(k) per token to validate allowed continuations; on modern kernels that adds ~3-10% latency for small models on GPU, more like 8-25% for larger models or when using CPU fallback. numbers vary by batch size and sequence length.
[01:23] Zoe: also important: constrained decoding limits sampling, so quality is deterministic but you lose some sampling-based creativity which is fine for strict JSON outputs. for tool calling where we want exact fields, it's usually a win.
[01:35] Priya: curious about batching. we want to batch 16-32 reqs to improve throughput, but we also need deterministic per-request outputs. does constrained decoding prevent batching?
[01:46] Maya: it complicates it but doesn't prevent it. two patterns: 1) synchronous token-synchronous batching where all requests proceed token-by-token together and you apply constraints per request, or 2) you break batches by 'blocking' requests that finish early so others continue - that reduces kernel efficiency. in our benchmarks, token-synchronous batching with constraints keeps batching benefits but you pay the constraint-check overhead per token for each slot. so p50 improves but p95 can degrade if you have stragglers or lots of varied-length outputs.
[02:20] Carlos: any interaction with KV cache? our policies sometimes feed long contexts (system + 2k user tokens). we rely on KV cache to avoid re-computation, but is constrained decoding compatible?
[02:32] Maya: yes, KV cache is orthogonal - it's the same attention/kv memory. constrained decoding doesn't touch the KV cache contents; it only filters next-token choices. that said, longer contexts increase decoding time per token a bit due to attention kernel cost and KV reads, so total latency increases. also note a side-effect: when using very long contexts, batching benefits decrease because memory pressure can cause more host-device transfers on some setups.
[02:58] Tom: what about quantization? we plan to run int8 quantized models to save memory and cost. does quantization change constrained-decoding behavior or output determinism?
[03:08] Maya: quantization affects model output distributions slightly; in our experience int8 (and 4-bit in some kernels) keep JSON structure accuracy high for deterministic decodes but can shift token probabilities near boundary cases. because constrained decoding forces valid tokens, it's robust, but you'll want to validate on your schema sets. perf wise, quantized kernels reduce per-token compute significantly - so overall latency often improves despite the constraint overhead. caveat: some quantized attention kernels have higher variance in latency on older GPUs.
[03:47] Aisha: from security perspective, if we run in our VPC or on-prem, do you still do constraint checks on our side? any PII leaving?
[03:56] Ben: for private deployments, all runtime logic (including constrained decoding) runs in your environment when you choose Private. Redwood's control plane is optional - logs and traces can be sent to your logging stack. we'll provide configs to disable any telemetry.
[04:12] Priya: good. what about tool/function calling itself - e.g., we call an internal service to validate account status. is that external latency included in the end-to-end SLO?
[04:22] Maya: we treat tool calls as additional steps in the request flow. there are two modes: synchronous inline calls (model triggers function, runtime awaits function output and continues decoding) or async where the model emits a call intent and you poll or push result back. Inline mode adds external network latency and blocks the request; our router can route tool calls to local sidecars in the VPC to minimize cross-network hops. for p95 guarantees we recommend local sidecars or pre-warmed function workers.
[04:56] Carlos: inline blocking worries me - it could spike p95 if our validation service is busy.
[05:00] Maya: exactly - that's why we suggest a) implement a local resilient sidecar with circuit-breaker, and b) set a short function timeout and fallback. Redwood's runtime supports automatic fallback to a cached or simpler model output if the function times out.
[05:14] Zoe: also note that constrained decoding + tool calling interacts: if the model must wait for a tool result before continuing the JSON structure, we can hold the open token stream; that means the decoder's state is preserved and resumed, so there's minimal recompute when the result returns, but you still have a wait.
[05:32] Tom: any microbenchmarks you can share?
[05:34] Maya: yes - quick numbers from our lab (internal, approximate):
- Baseline generation (no constraints, no tool calls), small open model, single request, p50 ~ 120ms, p95 ~ 320ms.
- Add constrained decoding (JSON schema simple), overhead +6-12% p50, +10-20% p95 depending on model size.
- Add inline tool call (local sidecar with 15ms response): end-to-end p50 ~ 150ms, p95 varies by tool variance.
- Batching 16x without constraints improves throughput 10-12x but increases single-request p95 due to queueing; with token-synchronous constrained decoding batching is still beneficial but constraint-check overhead scales linearly with batch width.

[06:30] Priya: curious about memory: KV cache footprint with batch 16 and 2k context - how much GPU memory?
[06:37] Maya: depends on model size and kv dtype; for a 7B-ish model with 2k context and batch 16 you'll see around 30-40GB KV memory on typical attention implementations. quantization reduces model weights but KV cache still uses fp16/32 depending on runtime; we have options to compress KV cache to reduce mem by ~30% at small CPU cost.
[06:58] Carlos: compression sounds promising. any tradeoffs?
[07:01] Maya: compression adds CPU overhead when serializing/deserializing during cold-starts or when we spill to host. it’s a tradeoff between peak GPU memory and small additional latency on cache access in pathological cases. for most steady-state workloads it's net positive.

[07:20] Tom: if we run Dedicated vs Private on-prem, what differences in latency should we expect?
[07:27] Ben: Dedicated hosted in Redwood DCs will have very low intra-cluster latency but goes over public cloud network to call your internal services unless you use secure peering. Private on-prem keeps all network local but you'll be limited by your local infra (GPU types, NVLink configs). Our shared numbers show on-prem can be slightly faster for tool-heavy workloads if you colocate services, but it requires more ops.

[07:48] Aisha: audit logs - do you capture token-level logs? this is sensitive for PCI use.
[07:54] Ben: by default we have token-level traces internally for debugging, but for Private deployments you can disable token logs and keep only structured request/response and hashes. Redwood offers KMS integration and HSM options for key management.

[08:09] Zoe: a couple of engineering notes: constrained decoding implementation choices matter - a trie-based token allowlist runs faster than regex-based validators. also precomputing token sets for schema prefixes reduces per-token compute. we've shared an RFC on this; we'll attach it.

[08:25] Carlos: let's talk acceptance criteria for pilot: 1) p50 < 200ms end-to-end including one inline tool call, 2) p95 < 600ms most traffic patterns, 3) 99% valid JSON outputs against our schema, 4) run 1k qps microbench for throughput.
[08:40] Maya: those are reasonable. for 1k qps we'll need Dedicated/GPU provisioning and token-synchronous batching tuned. we'll provide a benchmark plan.

[08:50] Ben: quick recap and next steps: we'll send the on-prem benchmark sheet and constrained decoding notes, schedule the 2-hour pilot kickoff, and exchange the security pack. action items captured. thanks everyone.

End transcript.
